title: NBA League Pass Rankings: Part 2
contentHtml:
Welcome to Part 2 of our 13th-annual NBA League Pass Rankings. Yesterday, we published Part 1, which outlined our methodology and revealed the bottom six teams: the Bucks, Clippers, Nets, Kings, Wiz, and Pelicans.

Today, we will continue our countdown with nos. 24 through 19. Reminder: We are publishing these rankings in five parts to mark the lead-up to the new season; once it tips off, The Lowe Post will convert to its normal cadence of one post per week.

Without further ado …

Subscribe now

24. Chicago Bulls (26)

The Bulls are new and young, and the algorithm scorns that combination—even when it includes the incendiary Caleb Wilson and the elbows-out, herky-jerky nastiness of Matas Buzelis; the novelty wears off when the losing compounds.

But the starting five of Josh Giddey, Norman Powell, Nic Claxton, Buzelis, and Wilson—perhaps the most viscerally exciting of the league’s star rookies—should absolutely fly from defense to offense, with Giddey galloping the ball up, Powell fanning to the arc, and Buzelis and Wilson running the wings as one of the most terrifying young open-court forward duos in recent memory. Those two might approach four combined blocks per game on defense.

This season should be about investigating how the like-sized trio of Giddey, Wilson, and Buzelis fits. Who will develop into an above-average 3-point shooter first—including on pull-up 3s? Who will have the ball most? Can Tiago Splitter unlock pick-and-roll combinations involving two of those three, even if defenses switch? (The Bulls’ starting five should be ultra-switchy in its own right.)

Buzelis and Wilson are central-casting second-side attackers, made (for now) to exploit gaps that someone else has opened instead of cracking those gaps themselves. How do the Bulls do that in the half court? Something to put in your back pocket: The floor has looked wide open for those slicing drives with Jalen Smith—a real stretch 5—starting in place of the injured Claxton in the preseason.

Noa Essengue and Dailyn Swain are swing pieces in Chicago’s latest (and truest) rebuild attempt. What are they? (I get nervous whenever Swain brings the ball up.) Could Leonard Miller—preseason star—finally kinda happen?

The Bulls’ core art and starting introductions are pristine. Please light all their black alternate jerseys on fire. And so long as broadcasters concoct every feed imaginable, why not add a Benny the Bull cam? He is one of maybe three mascots that might justify it—if only for his orgiastic popcorn explosions in the crowd.

Is Patrick Williams’s one-dribble pull-up the most depressing shot in basketball—the sad trombone of shots? It is a shoulder-sagging act of surrender. Is Isaac Okoro the league’s most confounding role player? One night, he looks like an archetypal 3-and-D sort. The next, he hits the side of the backboard and plays six minutes. How many consecutive corner 3s would Okoro have to hit before defenses pretended to guard him? Almost 100?

Tre Jones and Smith formed one of the NBA’s sneaky productive bench duos last season.

I’ll miss you, Stacey King. Keep making posters and pouring the hot sauce. There’s five Giddeys out there!
